original_value: End-to-end latency in remote-rendering systems can reduce user task performance. This notably includes aiming tasks on game streaming services, which are presently below the standards of competitive first-person desktop gaming. We evaluate the latency-induced penalty on task completion time in a controlled environment and show that it can be significantly mitigated by adopting and modifying image and simulation-warping techniques from virtual reality, eliminating up to 80% of the penalty from 80 ms of added latency. This has potential to enable remote rendering for esports and increase the effectiveness of remote-rendered content creation and robotic teleoperation. We provide full experimental methodology, analysis, implementation details, and source code.

result.paraphrase: End-to-end latency in remote-rendered systems can hurt user task performance. This is especially true for aiming tasks on game streaming services, which currently fall short of competitive first-person desktop gaming standards. In a controlled environment, we measure the latency-related penalty on task completion time and show it can be substantially reduced by adopting and adapting image- and simulation-warping methods from virtual reality, removing up to 80% of the penalty caused by 80 ms of added latency. This could help enable remote rendering for esports and improve remote-rendered content creation and robotic teleoperation. We include the full experimental methodology, analysis, implementation details, and source code.
